summary: Defines InMon Corporation's sFlow system for monitoring traffic in switched and routed networks, including its sampling mechanisms, its MIB, and the format of sample data sent to a collector.

eli5.summary: It's a method where a machine peeks at some of the passing cars to estimate how busy the road is.

questions: what is the sflow datagram format
subtitle: A sampling-based method for monitoring traffic in high-speed networks

tldr.problem: Network operators need to continuously monitor traffic on high-speed switched and routed networks to understand traffic patterns, but traditional continuous logging would consume too much memory and processing power.
tldr.mechanism: sFlow uses statistical packet sampling and periodic counter sampling to capture representative traffic data from network devices and send it to a central collector via UDP datagrams, using XDR encoding for a compact format.
tldr.outcome: sFlow enables efficient site-wide and network-wide traffic monitoring on Gigabit-speed and faster networks with very low overhead, making it practical to monitor tens of thousands of devices from a single collection point.

today: sFlow, defined in RFC 3176, remains a widely used method for traffic monitoring in switched and routed networks. It is deployed by many network operators and is supported in most commercial switches and routers. The sampling approach makes it practical to continuously monitor very high-speed networks and large numbers of devices with minimal impact on device performance. While the RFC is Informational rather than standards-track, sFlow has become a de facto standard in network management.

sections.title: What sFlow Does
sections.content:
sFlow is a technology for monitoring traffic in networks containing switches and routers. It was developed by InMon Corporation and defines three key parts: the sampling mechanisms used in an sFlow Agent (which runs on a switch, router, or stand-alone probe), the SFLOW MIB for controlling the agent via SNMP, and the format of sFlow Datagrams for sending samples to a central analyzer.

The system is designed to address the challenges of monitoring at high speeds (Gigabit and faster), scaling to manage tens of thousands of agents from a single point, and doing so with minimal cost to implement in switches and routers. An sFlow Agent embedded in a network device captures traffic samples and sends them immediately to an sFlow Analyzer for analysis.
sections.eli5: sFlow is a system where routers and switches sample some packets and send information about them to a central computer that watches the overall traffic patterns.

sections.title: Sampling Mechanisms
sections.content:
sFlow uses two forms of sampling. Statistical packet-based sampling captures a representative sample of switched flows. A flow is all packets received on one interface, routed, and sent to another interface. The sampling mechanism maintains a counter that decrements with each packet; when it reaches zero, a sample is taken and the counter is reset to a random value such that the average sampling rate equals the configured rate.

Time-based counter sampling periodically polls network interface statistics at configured intervals. The sFlow Agent combines flow samples and counter samples opportunistically into datagrams: when a flow sample is generated, the agent may add counter samples to the same datagram if they are due.

The sampling design ensures that any packet has an equal chance of being sampled regardless of the flow it belongs to, and that the sampling rate is maintained statistically over time. Samples include the total packet count and total sample count so the analyzer can calculate the effective sampling rate.
sections.eli5: The agent picks packets at random in a way that averages to a fixed sampling rate, like sampling every 1000th packet. It also regularly checks counters like 'how many packets came in on this port today.'

sections.title: sFlow Datagram Format
sections.content:
sFlow uses UDP to send sampled data to a collector, making datagrams unreliable but robust. The RFC specifies the datagram format using XDR (External Data Representation), a compact binary encoding simpler than ASN.1.

Each datagram includes the IP address of the agent, a sequence number, and an array of samples. Samples are either flow samples (containing packet information) or counter samples (containing interface statistics). Flow samples include a sequence number, source identifier, sampling rate, the total number of packets that could have been sampled, packet data (which may be full headers or extracted fields), and optional extended data like VLAN information or BGP routing details. Counter samples include interface counters (bytes, packets, errors, etc.) for various interface types (Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI, etc.).

The datagram is designed to allow multiple samples in each datagram for efficiency. Agents are free to batch samples but should not wait for buffers to fill; samples must be sent within 1 second. The use of UDP reduces memory requirements and provides robust delivery even under heavy traffic or denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: The sFlow message includes the sender's address, a serial number, and a list of packet samples and counter snapshots in a compact binary format. Many samples can go in one message.

sections.title: Management and Control
sections.content:
The SFLOW MIB provides an SNMP interface for configuring and managing sFlow agents. Managed objects include the agent's version string, IP address, and a table of samplers, one per data source (interface, VLAN, or physical entity).

For each sampler, an operator can configure the packet sampling rate (as a ratio like 1 in every N packets), counter sampling interval (how often to poll counters), maximum header size to copy, maximum datagram size, and the IP address and port of the collector. The MIB uses ownership strings to prevent configuration conflicts when multiple management entities might want to control the same sampler.

The RFC notes that SNMP security (via access control lists) is usually adequate in enterprise settings, but some situations (like WAN routers) may disable SNMP and use a command-line interface instead. The agent is free to adjust sampling rates to respect hardware limits and should convert requested rates to the closest achievable rate.
sections.eli5: The system uses standard SNMP network management to tell each device what sampling rate to use and where to send the data.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
sFlow does not provide built-in security mechanisms; instead, security relies on proper deployment and configuration. Control security depends on SNMP security (access control lists) or command-line access restrictions. Transport security is a concern because sFlow datagrams are unencrypted and vulnerable to eavesdropping; operators can mitigate this by creating a secure measurement network using VLANs or VPN tunnels. The analyzer should verify source addresses and check sequence numbers to detect spoofed datagrams.

Confidentiality is limited by the fact that traffic data can reveal details about individual users' network activity. Operators can limit visibility by reducing the header size captured, and packet sampling makes it nearly impossible to reconstruct individual user transactions. Access to the sFlow Analyzer should be carefully secured.
sections.eli5: Traffic samples can reveal what people are doing on the network. Operators should keep the sFlow data private and route it over secure paths.
